bull_thesis: Ipsos is the world's third-largest market-research firm (about 2.53 billion euros of 2025 revenue), and after a roughly 14% single-day fall it trades near 35.74 euros, or about 8x trailing earnings and a mid-to-high-single-digit multiple of free cash flow. That fall was not a profit warning: it followed the abrupt 30-31 July 2026 exit of CEO Jean-Laurent Poitou (replaced immediately by 15-year insider Kelly Beaver), which erased a roughly 31% post-earnings rally that had taken the stock to a 52-week high near 43 euros the week before. The bull case is that a cheap, cash-generative, low-leverage (about 0.5x EBITDA) franchise just got handed back at a discount on a governance event that does not change the earnings power. The operating business is genuinely inflecting: Q2-2026 organic growth rebounded to +3.0%, and for the first time since 2023 all three regions and all four audiences grew together, with China and Public Affairs (government/polling work) both turning positive. The high-margin do-it-yourself platform Ipsos Digital keeps compounding at 27-30% at roughly twice the group margin, which is the proof-point that AI is currently accretive, not destructive, for Ipsos. Management is returning cash (2.00 euro dividend up 8%, a 100 million euro buyback, 43 million euros already retired in H1). On a normalized ~316 million euro operating profit at 7-8x EV/EBIT, or ~10x forward earnings of about 4.5 euros, or a ~9% free-cash-flow yield on ~200 million euros of normalized FCF, base intrinsic value sits around 46 euros, roughly 29% above the shocked price, with a bull case near 55 euros if margins reach the 13.5% 2028 target and organic growth holds at 3%. bear_thesis: The cheapness is a fear-print for a reason. Ipsos is a low-single-digit grower (five-year revenue CAGR only +1.6%; 2025 organic growth just +0.6%) in an end market facing a genuine structural threat: generative AI and synthetic respondents can, over time, compress demand for human survey panels, which is the core of the business. Management itself concedes the moat now rests on proprietary panels and access to real respondents that AI players lack, which is the terminal-value question stated in its own words. The forecasting record is weak, with organic growth repeatedly landing below stated ambition and a 0-of-2 quarterly beat rate; the 2028 targets (3-4% organic, 13.5% margin) therefore deserve a discount. Governance is the fresh red flag: three CEOs (Page, then Poitou, now Beaver) and two CFOs inside roughly two years, with a CEO leaving one week after his first clean quarter and mid-way through the strategy he personally launched, framed thinly as 'personal projects.' # Forensic Dossier — Ipsos S.A. (IPS.PA, Euronext Paris)

*Prepared for the investment committee. Prices in euros (EUR). Live price €35.74 as of 2026-08-02, after a roughly 14% single-day fall from €41.66. Ipsos is the world's third-largest market-research and public-opinion firm (about €2.53 billion of revenue in 2025, close to 20,000 staff, 90 markets).*

## 1. Narrative Arc

Across the five calls on file (H1-2025 through H1-2026) the story moves through three distinct chapters.

**Chapter one — "reasonable return to growth" under the old guard (H1-2025, July 2025).** Then-CEO Ben Page framed a soft first half (1.5% total growth, Q2 organic just +0.7%, margin down to 8.3% from 10.1%) as a phasing story that would "strengthen during the rest of the year," and leaned on two fresh acquisitions — The BVA Family and infas — plus the high-margin do-it-yourself platform Ipsos Digital (growing 26%, roughly twice the group margin) as the growth engine. The subtext: buy growth through deals while the organic engine sputters.

**Chapter two — new CEO, new strategy (Q3-2025 Oct 2025 through FY-2025 Feb 2026).** Jean-Laurent Poitou arrives (September 2025), and the language pivots hard to transformation: a 50-year data heritage as "the fuel" for artificial-intelligence models, "speed" as the thing clients demand, and a promise of a full strategy — "Horizons" — unveiled 22 January 2026. FY-2025 landed at just +0.6% organic growth (well short of the ambition) but with margin held near guidance (12.8% before deal dilution). Horizons set medium-term targets: about 3-4% organic growth and a 13.5% operating margin by 2028, 14% thereafter, and €1.4 billion of cumulative free cash flow over five years.

**Chapter three — the turn, then the shock (Q1 and H1-2026).** Q1-2026 was ugly (organic −1.4%, Americas −4.1%) but management insisted the order book (+1%) supported a back-half acceleration. H1-2026 (23 July 2026) delivered the proof: Q2 organic growth rebounded to +3.0%, and for the first time since 2023 all three regions and all four audiences grew together. The market cheered — the stock ran about 31% to a 52-week high near €43. Then, roughly a week later (about 30-31 July 2026), the board announced Poitou's abrupt exit "to pursue personal projects," installing 15-year insider Kelly Beaver with immediate effect. The stock gave back the entire rally in a day.

Growth drivers quietly added and dropped along the way: Public Affairs (government/polling work) was the persistent drag through 2024-25 (down 8-15%), then flipped to a headline positive in Q2-2026 (+8%); China went from "structural difficulties" to "leading player, market-share gains"; and generative AI shifted from a cost/threat worry to a claimed growth lever via Ipsos Digital and Synthesio.

## 2. Claims vs Financials (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Return to growth… accelerating through the year" | 2025 organic +0.6%; H1-2026 +0.8%; Q2-2026 +3.0%. Multi-year revenue CAGR only +1.6%. | **Partly supported.** The Q2 inflection is real, but the base rate is anemic — this is a low-single-digit grower, not a compounder. |
| "Margin held; 13.5% by 2028" | 2025 operating margin 12.8% before deal dilution; H1-2026 down 40bp to 7.9% (seasonally the weak half); gross margin slipped 68.7%→67.7%. | **Supported but soft.** Margin is holding, not expanding yet; gross margin is under mix and acquisition pressure. |
| "Particularly strong balance sheet, 0.5x EBITDA" | Company-reported net debt €225M at June-2026 (down from prior year); our balance-sheet recompute puts net debt near €252M ex-lease / €351M including leases. Leverage genuinely low. | **Supported.** Leverage is modest whichever definition you use; this is not a distressed name. |
| "Record return to shareholders" | €2.00 dividend (up 8%), €100M buyback authorized, €54M of buybacks in H1 (€43M for cancellation). | **Supported.** Real cash returns against ~€1.5B market cap. |
| Delivering guidance | Beat 0 of 2 quarters (0%) in the screener; 2025 organic (+0.6%) came in below the earlier 2-3% ambition; FY-2026 guide trimmed from 2-3% to about 2%. | **Weak.** The forecasting track record is the soft spot — repeated organic shortfalls. |

The story is modestly *richer* than the trajectory justifies on growth (the Horizons narrative implies an acceleration the last five years of ~1.6% revenue CAGR has not shown), and roughly *fair* on cash and balance sheet.

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Declining-to-stabilizing, then destabilized by the CEO exit.** Ben Page (H1-2025) was defensive-optimistic ("reasonable return to growth… expecting it to strengthen"). Poitou's arrival injected offensive, strategic language ("no room for complacency," "we must embrace [AI] even more"). By H1-2026 the tone was genuinely more confident and specific — Poitou: growing on "all 4 fronts, and that's the first time… at least since 2023." Then the abrupt leadership change undercuts all of it: a CEO who launched a multi-year transformation in January leaving in July, one week after his first clean quarter, is a confidence event no transcript can offset. Language across the period shifted from offensive (growth/investment) toward a balance of both, with recurring defensive notes on cost control ("careful control on recruitment," "adapting our cost base").

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**Low-to-Medium.** The screener records a 0-of-2 beat rate, and the multi-year record shows organic growth repeatedly landing below stated ambition (2025 delivered +0.6% against a 2-3% frame). Management does telegraph seasonality honestly (H2 is structurally 70% of profit) and hit the 2025 *margin* target. But the recurring pattern — guide to acceleration, deliver low-single-digits — means the 2028 targets (3-4% organic, 13.5% margin) deserve a discount until proven. There is a mild sandbagging tell on margin (H1 always weak, H2 always carries the year) but no such cushion on the top line.

## 5. Analyst Pressure Points

Analysts (Bernstein, UBS, Berenberg, ODDO, Finance Connect) pushed repeatedly on three things: (1) the bridge from ~2% guided growth to the 3-4% 2028 target — management deflected to "the strategy will be disclosed" and "gradual acceleration"; (2) when the BVA/infas margin dilution reverses — answered consistently (18-24 months, fully absorbed by end-2026); (3) whether AI disintermediates the business — management reframed AI as complementary and a growth lever (panels/real respondents as the moat, Ipsos Digital at 2x margin). The unaddressed worry: durable organic acceleration in a world where clients can increasingly buy synthetic data. The CEO exit now adds a fourth, sharper question — execution continuity — that no prior call anticipated.

## 6. Red Flags / Green Flags

🔴 **Management churn.** Ben Page → Jean-Laurent Poitou (Sept 2025) → Kelly Beaver (July 2026) as CEO, plus a CFO change (Dan Levy → Olivier Champourlier). Three CEOs and two CFOs inside roughly two years is a governance-stability flag.
🔴 **CEO leaves one week after his first good quarter**, mid-way through the strategy he personally launched — the "personal projects" framing is thin, and the market read it as bad.
🔴 **Anemic organic growth** (five-year revenue CAGR +1.6%; 2025 +0.6%) against a structurally-questioned end market.
🔴 **Gross-margin drift** (68.7%→67.7%) on mix (lower-margin face-to-face Public Affairs) and dilutive deals.
🟢 **Genuine cash generation** and a cheap multiple (about 8x earnings, mid-single-digit to high-single-digit price-to-free-cash-flow depending on the FCF definition).
🟢 **Q2-2026 breadth** — all regions and audiences positive for the first time since 2023; China and Public Affairs both inflected up.
🟢 **Low leverage** (~0.5x EBITDA), €100M buyback, rising dividend — capital returns are real.
🟢 **New CEO is a 15-year insider** (Beaver ran UK/Ireland and UK Public Affairs) — continuity of the plan is more likely than a fresh strategic reset.

## 7. Hidden Signals

The most telling shift is how AI is discussed. Early calls treated it as a client-spend headwind (big-tech clients moving research budgets to product teams); by 2026 management reframed it as Ipsos's own lever — "synthetic respondents," Ipsos.Digital, Synthesio — while quietly conceding the moat now rests on *proprietary panels and access to real respondents* that AI players "do not have direct access to." That is the whole terminal-value question stated in management's own words: the panel/ground-truth asset is either the durable moat or the last line before disintermediation. Capital allocation language also hardened — from "over 100 acquisitions" as a growth reflex toward "internalization" of panels and GMS (globally managed services) as the margin story. And the halt/write-down of €11.6M of IT projects in H1-2026 signals the new regime repricing prior investment.

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING (turning).** The operating business inflected up in Q2-2026, but leadership just turned over again and the end market faces a genuine structural question. The single most important thing to weigh before sizing: **is the Q2-2026 organic reacceleration durable under a brand-new (if internal) CEO, or was it a phasing/order-book blip in a business whose five-year organic run-rate is barely positive?** The next hard read is Q3 results on 23 October 2026.

**Economic moat: NARROW.** Type: intangible brand plus a proprietary-panel/data-scale advantage and switching costs on large, multi-year public-sector and top-30 client relationships. Width judged by the evidence: returns are decent-not-fortress (ROIC ~9.5%, ROE ~12.9%) and gross margin is drifting down modestly — that is a narrow moat, not a wide one, and not clearly widening. **Moat trend: STABLE** — margins are being defended and are targeted to rise to 13.5% by 2028, but gross-margin mix pressure keeps it from widening.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL (not yet terminal).** The structural force is AI displacement of primary survey research — synthetic respondents and generative models compressing demand for human panels. Today this is net *accretive* for Ipsos (Ipsos Digital at ~27-30% growth and ~2x group margin; panels as AI training/ground-truth data), which is why the threat is material rather than terminal. But it is the dominant long-run risk and the reason the cheapness must be read carefully: this is a fear-print on a narrow-moat, slow-growth franchise, not a wide-moat compounder on sale. The discount is real; the durability is the open question.
